# `kill -9 -1` (also `-KILL -1`, `-s KILL -1`, `-- -1`) signals every
# process the user may signal, ending the session and everything in it
# (issue #750). A target token of exactly `-1` is the only shape this can
# key on, so `kill -1 1234` (SIGHUP to one pid) also asks: over-asking
# there costs one prompt, and the ambiguity is the flag/pid grammar's.
[[command]]
id = "kill-all-processes"
decision = "ask"
reason = "kill with pid -1 signals every process the user can signal, ending the whole session"
command = "kill"
# `exact` cannot normalise an integer, so zero-padded (`-01`, `-001`,
# `-0001`) and blank-padded spellings are listed; longer padding is a
# disclosed gap.
targets = [
    { exact = "-1" },
    { exact = "-01" },
    { exact = "-001" },
    { exact = " -1" },
    { exact = "-1 " },
    { exact = " -1 " },
    { exact = "-0001" },
    { exact = "  -1" },
    { exact = "-1  " },
]

# `killall5` signals every process outside its own session; `pkill`/`killall`
# with `-u`/`--user` and no narrowing pattern signal all of a user's
# processes. A pattern given alongside `-u` still asks (the rule cannot see
# whether one is present).
[[command]]
id = "killall5-all-processes"
decision = "ask"
reason = "killall5 signals every process outside its own session"
command = "killall5"

[[command]]
id = "pkill-user-processes"
decision = "ask"
reason = "pkill -u signals processes owned by a user, up to all of them"
command = "pkill"
required_flags = ["u|U|--user|--uid|--euid"]

[[command]]
id = "killall-user-processes"
decision = "ask"
reason = "killall -u signals processes owned by a user, up to all of them"
command = "killall"
required_flags = ["u|--user"]

# --remove-destination unlinks the destination node itself before copying
# — for a device node this deletes and replaces it (e.g. root's
# `/dev/null` becomes a regular file capturing everything subsequently
# "discarded" to it), so cp-write-device's except_targets below ("harmless
# in either role") doesn't hold here. Precedes cp-write-device so this
# narrower, more specific reason wins first-match on any overlap (both
# decide "ask", so this only affects which reason string surfaces).
[[command]]
id = "cp-remove-destination-device"
decision = "ask"
reason = "cp --remove-destination replaces the /dev/ node itself rather than writing into it"
command = "cp"
required_flags = ["--remove-destination"]
targets = [{ normalized_prefix = "/dev/" }]

# cp has no if=/of= flags to disambiguate source from destination, and
# target matching is membership-based (any resolved token), not positional
# — so unlike dd/dcfldd's precise strip="of=" targeting, this can't tell
# `cp /dev/sda backup.img` (reading a device, benign) from `cp file
# /dev/sda` (writing to one, destructive) apart from checking both
# candidate tokens against `/dev/`. decision="ask" (not the default Block)
# accounts for that ambiguity; except_targets carves out device nodes that
# are harmless in EITHER role (safe to read from AND to write to), so the
# everyday `cp /dev/urandom key.bin` idiom stays Allow while any other
# /dev/ target (source or destination) still asks. `-t`/`--target-
# directory=` are covered via `strip` (same precedent as tar's `strip =
# "-C"` above), unlike the shell-init-* family's plain target lists, which
# disclose that same gap as unfixed (#198, above) — this rule closes it
# instead since it has only one target to cover, not ~40. Appended here,
# not near dd-write-device, for the same reason as the shell-init-*
# family: `match_command`'s worst-wins scan (issue #399) means it can
# never shadow the stricter self-protect-config-cp-tilde Block above it,
# regardless of where it's declared.
[[command]]
id = "cp-write-device"
decision = "ask"
reason = "cp writing to (or reading an unlisted) /dev/ device may overwrite raw disk contents"
command = "cp"
targets = [
    { normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    # Bare "/dev" (no trailing slash) as its own token — the separated
    # `-t /dev sda`/`--target-directory /dev sda` form, where the value is
    # a standalone token `strip` can't reach (strip only matches a prefix
    # WITHIN one token, e.g. the glued `-t/dev` form below).
    { normalized = "/dev" },
    { strip = "--target-directory=", normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    { strip = "--target-directory=", normalized = "/dev" },
    { strip = "-t", normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    { strip = "-t", normalized = "/dev" },
]
except_targets = [
    { exact = "/dev/null" },
    { exact = "/dev/zero" },
    { exact = "/dev/urandom" },
    { exact = "/dev/random" },
]

# Issue #246: bash's `enable -f <sofile> [name]` dlopen()s an arbitrary
# shared object and registers its exported symbols as new shell builtins —
# native code loading via a file path, a fundamentally different shape from
# anything the exec-wrapper catalog (src/knowledge/) models (those are all
# "run the next argv word as a command"; this is "load and execute this
# file's machine code directly"). No `targets` needed: unlike dd/cp, the
# danger here is the mere PRESENCE of `-f` with any value at all, not which
# path it names — there is no safe/harmless sofile to except. `enable`
# WITHOUT `-f` never dispatches a trailing word as a command the way
# `builtin name args...` does (`enable rm -rf /` just fails trying to
# enable builtins literally named `rm`/`-rf`/`/`, none of which exist —
# nothing executes), so it deliberately does not belong in
# the exec-wrapper catalog (src/knowledge/), and this rule is scoped to the `-f` form only.
# This asymmetry — no live dispatch to over-match into — is also exactly
# why a plain `required_flags`-style rule is safe here but was rejected
# for `builtin`'s own `-f` form (issue #365): every shape this rule
# over-matches (e.g. `enable rm -rf /`) is already a no-op/error in a
# real shell, so over-blocking it costs nothing.
[[command]]
id = "enable-loadable-builtin"
reason = "enable -f dlopen()s an arbitrary shared object and runs its exported code as a new shell builtin"
command = "enable"
required_flags = ["f"]

# ksh93's `builtin` command shares this exact `-f <libname>` loadable-
# builtins shape (documented in ksh93's own manual: `builtin [-d|-f
# libname] name...`) — a real, verified second entry point to the same
# native-code-loading danger. NOT covered by a rule here: unlike
# `enable`, `builtin` is ALSO a dispatcher in the exec-wrapper catalog (src/knowledge/) (issue
# #245) — `builtin name args...` runs the shell builtin `name` with the
# REST of argv as `name`'s own arguments, not `builtin`'s own flags. A
# `required_flags = ["f"]` rule here false-matches any wrapped command
# that happens to use `-f`/`-rf`/etc. (confirmed: `builtin $CMD -rf /`
# wrongly matched during development of this rule, since `required_flags`
# scans the whole argv for the letter at ANY position, not specifically
# builtin's own leading flag). Issue #365 closes this with code-level
# detection instead — `crate::rules::builtin_loadable_library` (src/rules.rs),
# consumed by `src/gate.rs`'s rule 6e — scanning `builtin`'s own LEADING run
# of dash-prefixed tokens (stopping at the first bare name/`--`, which is
# the only place `builtin`'s own options can ever appear in ksh's grammar)
# for `f` in any cluster, rather than just the first tail token: ksh's
# option parser treats separated `-d -f lib` identically to clustered
# `-df lib`.

# Issue #426: a credential-shaped `NAME=` substring, in either an
# assignment name (`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=abc123 ls`) or a resolved argv
# word (`echo AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=abc123`) — command-agnostic, unlike
# every `[[command]]` rule above, since the sensitive part is the token
# itself, not which command it accompanies. `decision = "ask"`, not the
# type's own default `block`: the issue's own repro
# (`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=x aws s3 ls`) is also a normal credential-passing
# workflow, so a hard Block would be a false-positive-prone default for a
# heuristic this broad. Patterns are deliberately conservative substrings
# (`_KEY=` is NOT included — `SORT_KEY=`/`CACHE_KEY=` are common
# false positives); this list is user-config-tunable in spirit, but no
# user-facing `[[token]]` array exists yet (out of scope for #426, no
# issue currently open to add it).
[[token]]
id = "token-credential-shaped-assignment"
reason = "a credential-shaped NAME= token (secret/token/password) was found in an assignment or argument, and passing secrets on a command line exposes them via shell history and /proc"
decision = "ask"
patterns = [
    "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=",
    "_SECRET=",
    "_TOKEN=",
    "PASSWORD=",
]

[[command]]
id = "test-209-git-config-target"
reason = "test-only git targets rule"
command = "git"
targets = [{ normalized_prefix = "~/.config/shguard/" }]

[[command]]
id = "test-209-make-config-target"
reason = "test-only make targets rule"
command = "make"
targets = [{ normalized_prefix = "~/.config/shguard/" }]

[[command]]
id = "test-209-tar-config-target"
reason = "test-only tar targets rule"
command = "tar"
targets = [{ normalized_prefix = "~/.config/shguard/" }]

# shguard default blocklist (plan.md §1.1 stage 3).
#
# Embedded into the binary via `include_str!` (src/rules.rs) so the hook
# works with zero setup. Matching is mechanical and exact over the
# already-normalised argv (`crate::normalize`) — no regex over the raw
# command string.
#
# Schema
# ------
#
# [[command]] — matches one simple command's argv:
#   id               non-empty, unique string; the audit-trail id surfaced
#                    in a Block verdict's `matched_rule`.
#   reason           non-empty human-readable justification.
#   decision         optional: "block" (default) or "ask".
#   command          exact command name (argv[0]). Whitespace in `command`
#                    is ALWAYS interpreted as the subcommand-sugar split
#                    below — there is no way to exact-match a literal
#                    space-containing command name; accepted as a
#                    deliberate trade-off given how rare such command names
#                    are in practice. A multi-word value (e.g.
#                    "gh repo delete") is sugar: the first word becomes the
#                    command name and the remaining words are prepended onto
#                    `required_tokens`, so "gh repo delete" is equivalent to
#                    command = "gh", required_tokens = ["repo", "delete"].
#                    Don't also list those sugar words in `required_tokens`
#                    — they're prepended automatically, so an explicit
#                    `required_tokens` that literally starts with the same
#                    words (`required_tokens = ["repo", "delete"]` alongside
#                    this `command`) is rejected at load time rather than
#                    silently desugaring to the dead `["repo", "delete",
#                    "repo", "delete"]`.
#                    Mutually exclusive with `command_prefix` — exactly one
#                    of the two is required.
#   command_prefix   command-name prefix (e.g. "mkfs." for the mkfs.* family).
#                    Must not contain whitespace — the multi-word sugar above
#                    is only available via `command`.
#   required_flags   optional list of flag specs, ALL required (ANDed):
#                      - a single letter ("r") is a short flag, satisfied by
#                        a combined cluster ("-rf") or a separated token
#                        ("-r") — short-flag-aware.
#                      - a "-"-prefixed string ("-delete", "--recursive") is
#                        matched as an argv token, exact or with a "=value"
#                        suffix appended (GNU long-option convention, e.g.
#                        "--in-place" also matches "--in-place=.bak"; long
#                        options and BSD-style single-dash long flags are
#                        never letter-combinable). For a rule whose command
#                        is exactly "git" (deny/ask only, never allowlist
#                        entries), a "--long" flag is also satisfied by any
#                        non-empty prefix of it ("--mirr", "--upl=x"), since
#                        git accepts unambiguous long-option abbreviations
#                        (#582).
#                      - a "|"-separated spec ("r|--recursive") means "any
#                        one of these" (ORed) — use this so a rule can't be
#                        dodged by swapping a short flag for its long-option
#                        spelling (`rm --recursive --force /`). Each
#                        required_flags entry is still ANDed against the
#                        others; only the alternatives *within* one entry
#                        are ORed. An empty alternative ("r|", "|f") is a
#                        load-time error.
#   required_tokens  optional list of bare positional tokens (subcommands),
#                    ALL required (ANDed). Each must be non-empty and must
#                    NOT start with '-' (use required_flags for those).
#                    Matched as exact strings against argv[1..].
#   targets          optional list of target alternatives, ANY one hit by
#                    ANY argv token matches (ORed): `{ exact = "…" }` or
#                    `{ prefix = "…" }` (raw byte comparison, no path
#                    normalization), or `{ normalized = "…" }` /
#                    `{ normalized_prefix = "…" }` (issue #65: lexically
#                    normalizes the token — collapses `.`/`//`/trailing
#                    slashes, resolves `..` — before comparing, so `//`,
#                    `/.`, `~/..`, `../../../..`, etc. are recognized as
#                    the same target `/`/`~` a literal spelling would be).
#                    Exactly one of `exact`/`prefix`/`normalized`/
#                    `normalized_prefix`/`normalized_basename` is required
#                    per target entry. An optional `strip = "…"` (only
#                    legal alongside `normalized`/`normalized_prefix`/
#                    `normalized_basename`) requires the token to literally
#                    start with that string first (e.g. `strip = "of="`
#                    for `dd`'s `of=/dev/sda`, `strip = "-C"` for tar's
#                    attached `-C/` form) and normalizes only the
#                    remainder. A `normalized`/`normalized_prefix` value
#                    that itself normalizes to a pure relative ascent, an
#                    escape past `$HOME`, or something opaque (`""`,
#                    `~user`) is a load-time error — almost certainly a
#                    rule author's mistake. Deliberately NOT the default
#                    for `exact`/`prefix`: many targets aren't paths at all
#                    (`dd`'s `of=` prefix, a glob like `/*`, an
#                    `except_targets` URL prefix), and normalizing an
#                    `except_targets` entry would silently widen an allow.
#                    An empty/omitted `targets` list means "no target
#                    constraint" (e.g. `shred`'s "any target").
#
#                    `{ normalized_basename = "…" }` (issue #427) is a
#                    sixth shape: lexically normalizes the token like
#                    `normalized`/`normalized_prefix` do, but compares
#                    only its TRAILING path component (the filename) —
#                    independent of what directory prefix leads to it, or
#                    whether that prefix is even resolvable (an unresolved
#                    `../`, an unknown `~+`/cwd-relative anchor, etc. all
#                    still carry a certain filename). Matches when the
#                    trailing component equals the value exactly, OR
#                    starts with the value followed by a literal `.` — a
#                    dotenv-family suffix widening (`normalized_basename =
#                    ".env"` matches `.env`, `.env.local`,
#                    `.env.production`, anywhere: `.env`, `foo/.env.local`,
#                    `~/p/.env.production`, `/abs/.env`, `../.env` all
#                    match). A named user's home subdirectory
#                    (`~alice/.env`) matches too, unlike `normalized`/
#                    `normalized_prefix`: unresolvable and unreachable
#                    account names still spell a definite trailing
#                    filename, which is all this shape ever compares. The
#                    value itself must be a bare filename — no `/`, and
#                    not `.`/`..` — a load-time error otherwise. The
#                    dotted-suffix widening is broad by design: a
#                    `normalized_basename = "id_rsa"` rule also matches
#                    `id_rsa.pub`, intentionally (documented, not a bug).
#   except_targets   optional list of target alternatives, same
#                    `{ exact = "…" }` / `{ prefix = "…" }` shapes as
#                    `targets` (never `normalized`/`normalized_prefix`/
#                    `normalized_basename` — stays literal by policy, see
#                    above), plus an opt-in url_host shape
#                    `{ url_host = "…" }` (issue #102): parses
#                    the candidate as a real URL via the `url` crate
#                    (docs/adr/0002-url-crate.md) and compares its HOST
#                    component, not a string prefix of the raw text —
#                    closes the userinfo-spoofing gap `exact`/`prefix`
#                    matching can't (`http://localhost:pw@evil.example.com`
#                    shares a string prefix with `http://localhost:` but
#                    its real host is `evil.example.com`). Fails closed on
#                    an unparseable candidate (never excepted) — see the
#                    README's "Excepting specific targets" section for the
#                    full semantics, the IPv6-bracket requirement, and why
#                    it must REPLACE, not sit alongside, an existing
#                    `exact`/`prefix` entry for the same host to actually
#                    close the gap. `except_targets` is the opposite
#                    direction from `targets` (issue #30): the rule
#                    matches normally unless every candidate target
#                    token (the tokens `targets` matched, or every non-flag/
#                    `--flag=value`-value token when `targets` is empty,
#                    narrowed further by `value_flags` below) also matches
#                    an `except_targets` alternative. Never suppresses a
#                    match when the command's argv contains an unresolvable
#                    word (fail-closed). Example: `command = "curl"` with
#                    no `targets` plus `except_targets = [{ exact =
#                    "http://localhost" }, { prefix = "http://localhost:" },
#                    { prefix = "http://localhost/" }]` asks on every curl
#                    except a localhost target — see the README's
#                    "Excepting specific targets" section for why each
#                    alternative is boundary-anchored like this rather than
#                    a bare `{ prefix = "http://localhost" }`, and for the
#                    disclosed single-dash-attached-value gap
#                    (`-xhttp://evil.example.com`) this can't catch. When
#                    `targets` is empty, the sugar-derived subcommand words
#                    from a multi-word `command` are candidates too (e.g.
#                    command = "gh repo delete" with except_targets =
#                    [{prefix = "sandbox/"}] has candidates ["repo",
#                    "delete", "sandbox/x"]). This exact example — no
#                    except_targets alternative covers "repo" or "delete" —
#                    is a load-time error: those two words can never be
#                    excepted, so except_targets could never suppress the
#                    rule, which is provably-dead config rather than a
#                    working (if surprising) carve-out. The general shape
#                    (required_tokens + except_targets with empty targets)
#                    is not banned outright, though — if every
#                    required_tokens word is covered by some except_targets
#                    alternative (e.g. adding {exact="repo"} and
#                    {exact="delete"} to the list above, alongside the
#                    "sandbox/" prefix), the rule loads and the carve-out
#                    works correctly. Both shapes are covered by this
#                    project's own tests.
#   value_flags      optional list of flag names, each WITHOUT its leading
#                    `-`/`--` (issue #48): a single letter is a short flag
#                    ("o" for -o), anything longer is a long-option name
#                    ("exclude" for --exclude). Only meaningful alongside
#                    `except_targets` when `targets` is empty — a rule
#                    declaring `value_flags` with `targets` non-empty, or
#                    with no `except_targets` at all, is a load-time error
#                    (the field would otherwise silently do nothing). For
#                    each declared flag, its value — the following
#                    separated argv token, or a long flag's attached
#                    `--name=value` form — is consumed and excluded from
#                    the except_targets candidate set entirely, so a
#                    value-taking flag's own value (an output path, a
#                    format string, an exclude pattern) is never mistaken
#                    for the command's actual target. An undeclared flag's
#                    value still counts as a candidate (the existing
#                    fail-closed default). Example: `command = "curl"` with
#                    `value_flags = ["o", "w", "m"]` plus the
#                    `except_targets` above lets `curl -s -o /dev/null -w
#                    "%{http_code}" http://localhost:8787/` resolve cleanly
#                    instead of asking over -o's/-w's own values; `command
#                    = "rsync"` with `value_flags = ["exclude"]` plus a
#                    local-path `except_targets` list does the same for
#                    `rsync -a --exclude=".git" ./src/ ./dst/`. Declaring a
#                    flag here is a per-rule trust decision, same weight as
#                    an `except_targets` entry itself: only declare a flag
#                    whose value can never itself be (or point at) the
#                    thing this rule guards against — misdeclaring one is
#                    as much a bypass as a wrong except_targets pattern
#                    would be. A short flag glued into a combined cluster
#                    (`-so` for `-s -o`) is not recognised as the flag's
#                    bare spelling, so its value is not consumed (narrows
#                    the fix, never widens the gap); single-dash long
#                    options (`-cp` for a hypothetical `--cp`-shaped flag)
#                    aren't expressible either — only a bare `-x`/`--name`
#                    token is recognised. A bare `--` end-of-options
#                    terminator permanently turns off value_flags matching
#                    for every token after it, so a positional argument
#                    that happens to spell a declared flag's name past `--`
#                    (a real filename, not the flag) is never wrongly
#                    consumed. Don't declare an *optional*-argument flag
#                    (one that may or may not take a value depending on
#                    invocation, e.g. GNU `--color[=WHEN]`) — when such a
#                    flag appears bare, the next token is an unrelated
#                    positional that would be wrongly consumed as if it
#                    were the flag's value.
#   attached_value_flags  optional list of single ASCII letters, each
#                    WITHOUT its leading `-` (issue #47) — the opposite
#                    direction from `value_flags` above: a declared short
#                    flag's value glued directly onto it with no `=`
#                    separator (curl's `-xVALUE` short proxy-flag syntax)
#                    is by default invisible to except_targets entirely
#                    (indistinguishable from an ordinary combined
#                    short-flag cluster like `-sSL` by shape alone).
#                    Declaring the letter here makes that glued value a
#                    NEW except_targets candidate instead — this can newly
#                    suppress a match that would otherwise fire, the same
#                    opt-in-loosening posture except_targets itself
#                    already has. Load-time-error rules similar to
#                    value_flags but narrower — `targets` non-empty, or no
#                    `except_targets` at all, means the field would
#                    silently do nothing, same as value_flags; unlike
#                    value_flags, declaring `required_flags`/
#                    `required_tokens` instead of `except_targets` does
#                    NOT make it live, since this field only ever feeds
#                    the except_targets candidate walk, never the
#                    required_tokens floor value_flags also narrows. A
#                    letter declared in both `value_flags` and
#                    `attached_value_flags` is also a load-time error
#                    (opposite candidacy effects for the same flag). Only
#                    the exact leading `-<letter>` shape
#                    is recognised — a declared flag glued into a
#                    non-leading cluster position (`-sxVALUE`) is not
#                    recognised, and a bare declared flag with nothing
#                    glued after it (`-x` alone) never becomes an empty
#                    candidate. Example: `command = "curl"` with
#                    `attached_value_flags = ["x"]` plus the
#                    `except_targets` above makes `curl http://localhost
#                    -xhttp://evil.example.com` correctly ask instead of
#                    being wrongly excepted.
#
# [[pipeline]] — matches the shape of a whole pipeline (the ported
# curl|wget → sh installer-pipe pattern only; the general decode-fed-pipe
# gate is a later issue, plan.md §4):
#   id, reason       same as above.
#   decision         optional: "block" (default) or "ask".
#   sources          command names; an earlier pipeline stage's command
#                    name must be one of these.
#   sinks            command names; the pipeline's final stage's command
#                    name must be one of these.
#   sink_required_flags
#                    optional flag specs (same syntax as [[command]]'s
#                    required_flags: a bare short letter matched inside a
#                    cluster, a "-"-prefixed token, "|" alternation);
#                    every entry must be satisfied by the resolved sink's
#                    own arguments. Absent or empty = no flag constraint.
#                    For a git sink (including version-suffixed spellings
#                    such as `git2`), a "--"-prefixed token also matches any
#                    non-empty prefix of it (`--no-ver` for `--no-verify`);
#                    ambiguous prefixes, which git itself rejects, are
#                    over-matched to the rule's verdict.
#
# [[redirect]] — matches the target of an output/append redirection:
#   id, reason       same as above.
#   decision         optional: "block" (default) or "ask".
#   targets          REQUIRED, non-empty list of target matchers (same
#                    `{ exact = "…" }` / `{ prefix = "…" }` syntax).
#                    Unlike [[command]], an empty list is a load-time error.
#
# [[token]] — matches a literal substring against every assignment name
# (`NAME=`), every resolved argv word, and every raw word's own literal
# text (with each expansion/brace-alternative boundary kept from being
# straddled), of a simple command, a `for` clause's `in` word list, or an
# `[[ ]]` extended-test operand — independent of which command is being
# run (issue #426):
#   id, reason       same as above.
#   decision         optional: "block" (default) or "ask".
#   patterns         REQUIRED, non-empty list of literal, case-sensitive
#                    substrings (not regex). An empty list, or an empty
#                    or NUL-containing pattern string, is a load-time
#                    error.
#   deny_message     optional, same as [[command]].

# =====================================================================
# File/disk destruction
# =====================================================================

[[command]]
id = "rm-recursive-force-dangerous-target"
reason = "rm with recursive+force flags against a root-level, home, device, or find-placeholder target"
command = "rm"
required_flags = ["r|R|--recursive", "f|--force"]
targets = [
    { normalized = "/" },
    # `normalized` (not `exact`, matching the same exact->normalized
    # migration issue #267 already applied to the `{}` placeholder entries
    # below): `//*`, `/./*`, `/tmp/../*`, and `/*/` all lexically collapse
    # to the same single component `*` at the filesystem root and must
    # Block too, exactly like `/dev/sda` and its `//dev/sda`/`/./dev/sda`/
    # `/tmp/../dev/sda` spellings already do below. `/tmp/*` collapses to
    # `Abs(["tmp","*"])`, a different value, and correctly stays unmatched.
    # A `normalized` target component made only of glob metacharacters
    # matches every glob-only spelling of the same component: one starting
    # with `.` is the same target as `.*`, any other as `*` (issue #595,
    # see `canonicalize_glob_form` in src/rules.rs). So `/*` below also
    # covers the globstar `/**`, `~/*` covers `~/**`/`~/?*`/`~/[!.]*`, and
    # `~/.*` covers `~/.??*`/`~/.[!.]*`/`~/.**`/`~/.[a-z]*`; a partial
    # pattern counted as the whole glob is the fail-closed direction.
    { normalized = "/*" },
    { normalized = "~" },
    # issue #506: `~/*` wipes $HOME's writable contents exactly like bare
    # `~` above (`rm -rf` removes everything under it non-interactively
    # regardless of dotglob), so it belongs at the same tier for the same
    # reason -- NOT because of any config self-protection angle: bash's
    # default (non-`dotglob`) `*`/`**` never match a leading-dot name, so
    # this does not actually reach `~/.config` on its own.
    { normalized = "~/*" },
    # `~/.*` is a leading-dot glob: unlike `~/*` above, it DOES expand to
    # $HOME's leading-dot entries (`.ssh`, `.aws`, `.gnupg`,
    # `.config/shguard`) even without `shopt -s dotglob`, since a leading
    # `.` in the glob pattern itself always matches a leading-dot name.
    # `rm -rf` non-interactively wipes every one of them, and this is the
    # one `~/*`-family spelling that genuinely reaches shguard's own
    # config directory (see `self-protect-config-ancestor-rm-tilde`/
    # `-mv-tilde` below, which are Ask-tier). Without this entry
    # `rm -rf ~/.*` would only reach those Ask-tier self-protect rules,
    # weaker than the Block `rm -rf ~/*` already gets. This is the
    # authoritative explanation of the leading-dot glob family; the
    # other entries below point back here. The "safe" spellings it also
    # covers (`.[!.]*`, `.??*`, `.[^.]*` skip both `.` and `..`; `.?*` may
    # match `..` (bash < 5.2)) still match `.ssh`/`.gnupg`/`.config`, so
    # they delete the same set.
    { normalized = "~/.*" },
    { normalized = "." },
    # issue #453: `./*` and bare `*` both lexically normalize to
    # `Rel{ascent:0, comps:["*"]}` — a different value from `.`'s
    # `Rel{ascent:0, comps:[]}` above, so they need their own entry. GNU rm
    # actually *refuses* `rm -rf .` ("refusing to remove '.'"), making
    # `./*`/`*` the spelling that really deletes the current directory's
    # contents; this keeps both at the same tier as `.`.
    # The globstar `**`/`./**` deletes the current directory's contents
    # exactly like `*`/`./*` (issue #506) and is covered by this entry.
    { normalized = "*" },
    # Same leading-dot glob reasoning as `~/.*` above, for the cwd-relative
    # spelling (`cd ~ && rm -rf .*`): `.*` and its glob-only siblings
    # match every leading-dot entry in the current directory regardless
    # of `dotglob`.
    { normalized = ".*" },
    # ".."/"../" (previously separate `exact` entries) are subsumed by
    # "/"'s pure-ascent widening (issue #65): `{ normalized = "/" }` also
    # matches any token that lexically normalizes to a pure relative
    # ascent with no remaining components (`Rel{ascent>=1, comps:[]}`),
    # which both ".." and "../" do — see src/rules.rs's `TargetMatcher::
    # NormalizedExact` match arm.
    { normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    # `{}` is `find -exec`/`-execdir`/`-ok`/`-okdir`'s own placeholder for
    # "whatever path find matched" (issue #72) — statically as uncontrolled
    # a target as `/`: `find -exec rm -rf {} \;` deletes every match,
    # regardless of the search root. shguard's `find -exec` recursion
    # (`crate::gate::scan_recursable_slots`) feeds the payload's literal
    # `{}` text straight into this same rule rather than trying to
    # special-case it, so this target entry is what makes that recursion
    # actually catch the canonical "delete everything found" pattern.
    # `normalized` (not `exact`, issue #267): `find` substitutes `{}`
    # anywhere inside a word, so `./{}`/`{}/`/`x/../{}` all still
    # resolve to the matched path and must Block too. `normalized`
    # matches any token that lexically collapses to the single component
    # `{}`, while still leaving a token that resolves to a genuinely
    # different path (`{}.`, `{}.bak`, `x{}`, `/tmp/{}`) unmatched.
    { normalized = "{}" },
    # The absolute re-root of the same evasion: when `find`'s search root
    # is absolute, matches are absolute too, so `/{}` substitutes to
    # `//x/foo` — the matched path itself — and deletes every match. That
    # token collapses to `Abs(["{}"])`, which `normalized = "{}"`
    # (`Rel{ascent:0, comps:["{}"]}`) cannot see, so it needs its own
    # entry; `//{}`/`/./{}`/`/../{}` collapse here too. With a relative
    # search root this spelling instead deletes `/<match>` at the
    # filesystem root, which is no safer.
    { normalized = "/{}" },
    # `~/{}` collapses to `Home(["{}"])`, a third anchor the two entries
    # above cannot reach. It deletes every match whenever the cwd is
    # `$HOME` and the search root is relative (`~/{}` substitutes to
    # `$HOME/./foo`). Unlike `/{}`, that precondition is invisible in the
    # command text, so this entry is fail-closed rather than exact — the
    # only thing it costs is a literal `$HOME/{}` file, which does not
    # occur in practice.
    { normalized = "~/{}" },
]

# issue #453: `rm -r` (recursive, no `-f`) against a root-level or device
# target is still non-interactively destructive — GNU/BSD `rm` only prompts
# for write-protected files, and only on a tty, so `rm -r /*` deletes every
# writable file under `/` unattended. `~` is deliberately NOT included here:
# `self-protect-config-ancestor-rm-tilde` below already floors bare
# `rm -r ~` (and, since issue #506, `~/*`) to Ask. `.`/`*` are out of
# this issue's stated scope (root/device targets only) and stay Allow.
# issue #506 extended this rule's own targets below with find's `{}`
# placeholder family, the same unattended-destruction risk through a
# different (uncontrolled, not literal) target -- `reason` below is worded
# to cover both shapes, mirroring the sibling `-rf` rule's own wording.
[[command]]
id = "rm-recursive-dangerous-target"
reason = "rm -r against a root-level, device, or find-placeholder target deletes every writable file there, without needing -f"
command = "rm"
required_flags = ["r|R|--recursive"]
targets = [
    { normalized = "/" },
    { normalized = "/*" },
    { normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    # issue #506: `find -exec rm -r {} \;`-style recursion achieves the
    # same unattended, writable-file-tree destruction as the root/device
    # targets above through find's own `{}` placeholder rather than a
    # literal dangerous path — the same reasoning `rm-recursive-force-
    # dangerous-target`'s sibling `{}`/`/{}`/`~/{}` entries already apply,
    # but reachable here without `-f`: `rm -r <dir>` alone still removes a
    # directory's writable contents non-interactively, it only prompts for
    # write-protected files on a tty. See that rule's own doc for the
    # collapse semantics these three entries share.
    { normalized = "{}" },
    { normalized = "/{}" },
    { normalized = "~/{}" },
]

# `-r`/`-R` is unnecessary for `rm -f {}` (no `-type f` needed either) to
# reach the dangerous property this rule targets — every matched FILE
# unrecoverably deleted, the same file-deletion effect `find -delete` has:
# `find`'s own `{}` placeholder resolves to one matched path at a time, so
# a plain-file match is fully removed by `-f` alone, and a directory match
# simply fails `rm` without `-r` (unlike `-rf {}`, which also removes a
# matched directory and everything under it — a strictly worse class,
# already covered by the sibling rule above). Both this rule and
# `rm-recursive-force-dangerous-target` above are Block, so
# `match_command`'s worst-wins tie-break (issue #399) keeps whichever is
# declared first, and `rm -rf {}` keeps reporting that rule's id.
# Deliberately targets ONLY `{}`, not the sibling rule's `/`/`~`/`/dev/`
# set above: without `-r`, `rm -f` can never remove a directory, so
# `rm -f /` or `rm -f ~` alone isn't the same destructive class and would
# be a false positive here. issue #140
[[command]]
id = "rm-force-find-placeholder-target"
reason = "rm -f against find's own {} placeholder removes every matched file, unrecoverably, the same effect find -delete has"
command = "rm"
required_flags = ["f|--force"]
# `normalized`, not `exact` (issue #267), plus the `/{}` and `~/{}`
# re-roots: see the sibling rule above for the collapse semantics all
# three entries share.
targets = [
    { normalized = "{}" },
    { normalized = "/{}" },
    { normalized = "~/{}" },
]

[[command]]
id = "find-delete"
reason = "find with -delete removes every matched file, unrecoverably"
command = "find"
required_flags = ["-delete"]

# Issue #141: dd's of= target only covered /dev/*, unlike
# redirect-overwrite-device-or-critical-file/tee-write-device-or-
# critical-file above, which also cover /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow — dd
# writing the same destructive content (e.g. zero bytes from /dev/zero)
# to a critical file outside /dev/ is exactly as destructive, same tool
# family, but fell through every blocklist rule. Only /etc/passwd/
# /etc/shadow are added here (not the redirect/tee list's specific
# per-vendor /dev/ prefixes) since dd-write-device's existing blanket
# `normalized_prefix = "/dev/"` already covers ALL of /dev/, strictly
# broader than that per-vendor list.
[[command]]
id = "dd-write-device"
reason = "dd writing directly to a raw block device or critical system file destroys data"
command = "dd"
targets = [
    { strip = "of=", normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    { strip = "of=", normalized = "/etc/passwd" },
    { strip = "of=", normalized = "/etc/shadow" },
]

# dcfldd is a drop-in dd variant (forensic imaging tool) with identical
# if=/of= semantics — same strip="of=" precision and critical-file parity
# as dd-write-device above, so no cp-style source/dest ambiguity here.
[[command]]
id = "dcfldd-write-device"
reason = "dcfldd writing directly to a raw block device or critical system file destroys data"
command = "dcfldd"
targets = [
    { strip = "of=", normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    { strip = "of=", normalized = "/etc/passwd" },
    { strip = "of=", normalized = "/etc/shadow" },
]

# Issue #136: rsync/mv/install writing a regular file's bytes onto a /dev/
# device special file is the same destructive effect as the already-Block
# dd/tee/redirect shapes, but none of these three had ANY /dev/* coverage.
# Unlike cp-write-device (#123, decision="ask"): that rule's source-role
# false-positive is common daily usage (`cp /dev/urandom key.bin`) for
# which no comparable idiom exists here — nobody routinely reads FROM
# `/dev/sda`/`/dev/null`/etc. as an rsync/mv/install SOURCE — so these
# three Block outright, same posture as dd/dcfldd above. The one real
# common idiom is `/dev/shm` (tmpfs scratch space: `mv build.tar
# /dev/shm/`, `rsync -a src/ /dev/shm/scratch/`), carved out via
# except_targets (both the bare-directory and prefixed spellings) exactly
# so that daily-usage break doesn't recur here.
#
# Reason wording deliberately avoids dd's "overwrites raw disk contents":
# mv/rsync's default same-filesystem behavior REPLACES the device node
# itself (rename, mknod-recoverable) rather than opening and streaming
# bytes into it the way dd/cp do — but losing the node out from under a
# running system is just as severe either way, and the issue's own
# framing puts this in the dd/tee severity class regardless of mechanism.
# (cp-remove-destination-device, #123, has the identical node-replacement
# effect but inherits cp's ask-tier posture from the rest of that rule
# family; these three have no such common-idiom pressure holding them to
# ask.)
#
# mv/install support cp's own -t/--target-directory= flags (rsync does
# not) — mirrors cp-write-device's full six-entry target list, same gap
# class fable found there (#330). Known gaps, not fixed here, same
# disclosed classes as cp-write-device/rsync-delete-dangerous-target: a
# cluster-glued short flag (`-vt/dev/sda`) and a GNU long-option
# abbreviation (`--target-dir=/dev/sda`) both bypass the -t/--target-
# directory= coverage above (issue #214's class). Separately, the
# except_targets carve-out below only ever sees the RAW candidate token —
# it doesn't know about `strip`, so the ATTACHED `--target-directory=
# /dev/shm` and GLUED `-t/dev/shm` forms still Block despite the except
# existing for the plain-positional spelling (the SEPARATED `-t /dev/shm`
# form does Allow: its value is its own token, matched and excepted like
# any other candidate, `strip` never enters into it there). Over-strict,
# not a security hole, left as a usability gap rather than widening
# except_targets' own raw-literal-only contract (see this file's own
# except_targets docs
# near the top) to understand `strip`.
[[command]]
id = "mv-write-device"
reason = "mv replacing a /dev/ device node (or overwriting into it) has the same destructive effect as dd/tee/redirect writing to a device"
command = "mv"
targets = [
    { normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    { normalized = "/dev" },
    { strip = "--target-directory=", normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    { strip = "--target-directory=", normalized = "/dev" },
    { strip = "-t", normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    { strip = "-t", normalized = "/dev" },
]
except_targets = [{ exact = "/dev/shm" }, { prefix = "/dev/shm/" }]

# /dev/stdin also stays Allow: `curl ... | sudo install -m755 /dev/stdin
# /usr/local/bin/x` is a common install idiom, and writing FROM stdin's fd
# never touches a disk device node the way the other /dev/* targets do —
# safe in the write role too, unlike the other node/device paths above.
[[command]]
id = "install-write-device"
reason = "install replacing a /dev/ device node (or overwriting into it) has the same destructive effect as dd/tee/redirect writing to a device"
command = "install"
targets = [
    { normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    { normalized = "/dev" },
    { strip = "--target-directory=", normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    { strip = "--target-directory=", normalized = "/dev" },
    { strip = "-t", normalized_prefix = "/dev/" },
    { strip = "-t", normalized = "/dev" },
]
except_targets = [
    { exact = "/dev/shm" },
    { prefix = "/dev/shm/" },
    { exact = "/dev/stdin" },
]

# rsync has no -t/--target-directory= flag (unlike mv/install above) —
# plain prefix targeting only. Bare "/dev" (no trailing slash, e.g. `rsync
# -a src/ /dev`) is a disclosed, undesigned residual, same as
# rsync-delete-root-or-device and rm-recursive-force-dangerous-target near
# the end of this file. Left unfixed deliberately, not merely undesigned:
# adding it would also need `--exclude`'s separated VALUE token
# (`--exclude /dev`, a real backup-script idiom excluding /dev from a
# recursive copy) to stop being misread as a positional target first —
# membership matching can't yet tell a flag's value from an ordinary
# operand (no `value_flags` support for a rule with a non-empty `targets`
# list — see this module's own value_flags docs), so `--exclude /dev/pts`
# in the textbook `rsync -aAX / /backup --exclude /dev/pts ...`
# full-system-backup idiom already Blocks via the plain `/dev/` prefix
# target above; adding bare "/dev" would make that worse, not better.
# Overlaps decision-identically (Block) with rsync-delete-root-or-device
# on `rsync --delete src/ /dev/sda`; only the reported reason differs
# depending on which rule happens to match first.
[[command]]
id = "rsync-write-device"
reason = "rsync replacing a /dev/ device node (or overwriting into it) has the same destructive effect as dd/tee/redirect writing to a device"
command = "rsync"
targets = [{ normalized_prefix = "/dev/" }]
except_targets = [{ exact = "/dev/shm" }, { prefix = "/dev/shm/" }]

[[command]]
id = "truncate-zero"
reason = "truncate -s zeroes/truncates the target file's contents in place"
command = "truncate"
required_flags = ["s|--size"]

# Issue #131: -r/--reference=RFILE sets the target's size to match RFILE's
# size instead of an explicit number — the target unconditionally takes on
# a size it didn't choose (shrunk and data-truncated, or grown and
# NUL-padded), the same unrecoverable content-destruction effect as -s,
# regardless of what RFILE actually is (a separate rule, not merged into
# truncate-zero above, mirrors how rm-recursive-force-dangerous-target and
# rm-force-find-placeholder-target stay two rules for one command rather
# than one rule with an OR'd reason that fits neither flag family well).
# Known gap, same as truncate-zero above: GNU's unambiguous long-option
# prefix matching (`--ref` alone works against real GNU truncate) isn't
# enumerable by a finite required_flags list — see rsync-delete-root-
# or-device's comment near the end of this file for the same class.
[[command]]
id = "truncate-reference"
reason = "truncate -r/--reference sets the target's size to match a reference file's size, unconditionally overwriting its contents in place"
command = "truncate"
required_flags = ["r|--reference"]

[[command]]
id = "shred"
reason = "shred overwrites and unlinks its target, defeating recovery"
command = "shred"

[[command]]
id = "mkfs-any-filesystem"
reason = "mkfs.* formats a filesystem, destroying all data on the target"
command_prefix = "mkfs."

[[command]]
id = "mke2fs-any-filesystem"
reason = "mke2fs is the implementation behind mkfs.ext*, formatting a filesystem and destroying all data"
command = "mke2fs"

[[command]]
id = "mkdosfs-any-filesystem"
reason = "mkdosfs is the implementation behind mkfs.vfat/mkfs.msdos, formatting a filesystem and destroying all data"
command = "mkdosfs"

[[command]]
id = "mkntfs-any-filesystem"
reason = "mkntfs is the implementation behind mkfs.ntfs, formatting a filesystem and destroying all data"
command = "mkntfs"

[[command]]
id = "mkswap-any-device"
reason = "mkswap overwrites the target device's/partition's signature to initialize it as swap space, destroying any existing filesystem or data"
command = "mkswap"

# wipefs's default (no flags) is informational — it only lists existing
# signatures without modifying anything. -a/--all and -o/--offset are the
# two ways to actually erase one, so (unlike mkswap-any-device above,
# always destructive) this is flag-gated rather than a bare command block;
# same shape as truncate-zero's required_flags above.
[[command]]
id = "wipefs-any-device"
reason = "wipefs -a/-o erases a device's/partition's filesystem or partition-table signature, destroying any existing filesystem or data"
command = "wipefs"
required_flags = ["a|--all|o|--offset"]

# blkdiscard has no informational default mode: bare `blkdiscard <device>`
# discards the whole device immediately, same "any bare target is
# dangerous" shape as shred above.
[[command]]
id = "blkdiscard-any-device"
reason = "blkdiscard discards (TRIMs) the target device's contents, destroying any existing filesystem or data"
command = "blkdiscard"

# issue #453: util-linux mkfs defaults to ext2 when -t/--type is omitted, so
# a bare `mkfs <device>` is exactly as destructive as `mkfs -t ext4 <device>`
# — it has no informational default mode besides -V/--help, same "any bare
# invocation is dangerous" shape as shred/blkdiscard above.
[[command]]
id = "mkfs-dispatcher-any-filesystem"
reason = "mkfs formats a filesystem (ext2 by default without -t/--type), destroying all data on the target"
command = "mkfs"

# tar extraction with -C/--directory into / or ~ overwrites arbitrary paths
# with archive contents. Two rules: the block rule requires an explicit
# extract flag so a benign `tar -cf backup.tar -C src .` (create, not
# extract) never matches; the ask rule below drops that requirement to
# also catch the dash-less old-style invocation form (`tar xf a.tar -C /`),
# where `x` never appears as its own `-`-prefixed token. `match_command`
# is worst-wins (issue #399), so the block rule outranks the ask rule on
# any overlap regardless of declaration order.
#
# Known limitations (same disclosure stance as the curl `-xURL` gap above
# and the `git -C <path>` gap in src/rules.rs):
#   1. Non-root dangerous directories (`-C /etc`, `-C /usr`, …) are not
#      caught: a `prefix = "/"` target would also hit ordinary `-C /tmp/...`
#      extractions, which is too many false positives for this rule.
#
# (Former item 1, the full old-style clustered invocation `tar xfC a.tar /`
# not being caught at all — `short_cluster_chars` returns an empty set for
# a dash-less token, so `xfC` never satisfied `required_flags` the way
# `-xfC` would — is fixed as of issue #67: `tar_dashless_rewrite`
# (src/rules.rs) rewrites a dash-less `x`+`C` cluster into the equivalent
# dashed tokens before this rule's own `required_flags`/`targets` ever see
# it, scoped strictly to `tar`'s own calling convention rather than a
# generic `FlagMatcher` change.)
#
# (Former item 3, `-P`/`--absolute-names` letting an archive member's own
# absolute path bypass `-C` entirely, is addressed as of issue #68 by the
# separate `tar-absolute-names-ask` rule below — it can only ever be `ask`,
# never `block`, since the actual danger lives inside the archive's own
# member paths, invisible to a command-line-only analyzer.)
#
# (Former item 4, path-normalization bypass via `-C //`/`-C /.`/`-C ~/..`/
# `-C ../../../..`, is fixed as of issue #65: the `normalized`/
# `normalized_prefix`/`strip` target forms below lexically normalize before
# comparing, so every one of those spellings now resolves to the same `/`/
# `~` target a literal spelling would. Still not tar-specific, and still
# shared by every rule using the new forms.)
#
# Why the target list is asymmetric — `-C/`/`--directory=/` are listed but
# `-C~`/`--directory=~` are not. Under POSIX/bash defaults, tilde expansion
# only fires at the start of a word, or after `=` in a word that is itself
# a valid variable assignment; a `-`-prefixed flag token is neither, so
# `-C~` and `--directory=~` reach tar as a literal `~` (verified: `printf
# '[%s]' -C~ --directory=~ ~` prints `[-C~] [--directory=~] [/Users/…]`),
# and tar does no tilde expansion of its own. Those forms chdir into a
# directory *named* `~` relative to the cwd, never `$HOME` — matching them
# would be a false positive under the shells most invocations actually
# run under. `/` needs no expansion to mean the root directory, which is
# why its attached forms do belong here.
#
# `-C~` stays excluded even accounting for the caveat below (re-verified
# live under zsh 5.9 with `magic_equal_subst` set: `-C~` is still
# literal — the option only ever matches an `=`-shaped word, and `-C~` has
# no `=`). `--directory=~`/`--directory=~user` do NOT get a symmetric
# certain-match/hard-Block target the way `--directory=/` does, though:
# issue #115 found that zsh's `magic_equal_subst` option (off by default,
# but some `.zshrc`s set it) extends tilde/parameter expansion to ANY
# `word=value`-shaped argument, not just a genuine variable assignment —
# so under that option, `--directory=~`/`--directory=~user` DO tilde-
# expand (verified live: `zsh -o magic_equal_subst -c "printf '[%s]'
# --directory=~"` prints the real `$HOME`, not the literal string).
# Since shguard cannot observe the invoking shell's options, this can only
# ever be flagged, never proven either way — handled by a dedicated
# Ask-only floor (`CommandRule::matches_directory_equals_tilde_floor` /
# `crate::gate::scan_directory_equals_tilde_floor`) rather than a `targets`
# entry, specifically so it floors without ever inheriting this rule's own
# (often `Block`) decision the way a certain match would. Issue #134 pairs
# the same magic_equal_subst uncertainty with `~+`/`~-`/`~N` directory-
# stack tilde forms attached the same way (`--directory=~+`) — floored by
# `CommandRule::matches_dirstack_equal_subst_floor`. Issue #128 closes the
# GNU long-option-abbreviation gap both floors previously shared with
# #214 (`--dir=~+` now canonicalizes to `--directory=~+` before either
# floor's own `--directory=` strip-string match ever runs, via
# `rules::tar_long_option_abbrev_rewrite` — see that function's own docs).
# `directory`/`extract`/`get` are the only long options these two
# directory rules match on (the sibling `tar-absolute-names-ask` rule's
# own `--absolute-names` gets the same rewrite too — see
# `tar_long_option_abbrev_rewrite`'s own docs for the full option list);
# the disclosed #214-class gap remains for `mv`/`install`/`cp`'s
# `--target-directory=` below, untouched by #128.
[[command]]
id = "tar-extract-over-root-or-home"
reason = "tar extraction with -C/--directory into / or ~ overwrites arbitrary system/home paths with archive contents"
command = "tar"
required_flags = ["x|--extract|--get", "C|--directory"]
targets = [
    { normalized = "/" },
    { strip = "-C", normalized = "/" },
    { strip = "--directory=", normalized = "/" },
    { normalized = "~" },
]

[[command]]
id = "tar-directory-root-or-home"
decision = "ask"
reason = "tar with -C/--directory pointed at / or ~ operates far outside the working directory"
command = "tar"
required_flags = ["C|--directory"]
targets = [
    { normalized = "/" },
    { strip = "-C", normalized = "/" },
    { strip = "--directory=", normalized = "/" },
    { normalized = "~" },
]

# -P/--absolute-names disables tar's default stripping of a leading `/`
# from archive member paths, so a member path like `/etc/passwd` (embedded
# in the archive itself, not visible on the command line) gets written to
# that absolute path verbatim, regardless of -C. No targets at all — the
# danger is invisible to a command-line-only analyzer, so this can only
# ever be ask, never block; -P alone doesn't prove a dangerous archive.
[[command]]
id = "tar-absolute-names-ask"
decision = "ask"
reason = "tar -P/--absolute-names lets archive member paths carry an absolute destination, bypassing -C/--directory entirely"
command = "tar"
required_flags = ["x|--extract|--get", "P|--absolute-names"]
# -C/--directory always takes the next argv word as its value, so a quoted
# unresolved word there (`-C "$DIR"`) is a directory, never a hidden `-P`
# (issue #579). Only the separated bare form is recognised.
value_flags = ["C", "directory"]

# =====================================================================
# Git — destructive/bypass operations
# =====================================================================

[[command]]
id = "git-push-force"
reason = "git push --force/-f (or an equivalent +-prefixed refspec, e.g. `git push origin +main`) overwrites remote history; --force-with-lease is the safe alternative"
command = "git"
required_tokens = ["push"]
required_flags = ["f|--force"]

# issue #452: a `+`-prefixed refspec (`git push origin +main`, `git push
# +HEAD:main`) is the same force push with no `-f`/`--force` flag at all —
# `required_flags` has nothing to match. `src/gate.rs`'s
# `git_push_plus_refspec` detects this structurally and reuses this rule's
# own id/reason/deny_message rather than declaring a second one here.

[[command]]
id = "git-reset-hard"
reason = "git reset --hard irreversibly discards uncommitted changes"
command = "git"
required_tokens = ["reset"]
required_flags = ["--hard"]

# Blocks all invocations including `git clean -n` (dry-run preview) —
# intentional: matches the dotfiles hook's behavior, and the dry-run form
# is harmless enough that a false-block here is low-cost.
[[command]]
id = "git-clean-any"
reason = "git clean permanently deletes untracked files"
command = "git"
required_tokens = ["clean"]

# -n is --no-verify for `git commit` only (for `git push` it means --dry-run).
# Known false-positive edge: a `-m` message argument starting with `-` and
# containing 'n' may trigger (same class of imprecision as the dotfiles hook).
# `value_flags` (issue #146) tells the unresolved-word floor that `-m`'s
# value is a value, not a candidate for `-n|--no-verify` — this is what
# lets `git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF' ... EOF)"` (a heredoc commit message)
# resolve to Allow instead of Ask. Only the separated bare-flag form (`-m
# msg`/`--message msg`) is covered: a `-am` combined-short-flag cluster and
# an attached `--message=$(...)` form both still Ask, by design (see
# `ValueFlag`'s own docs in src/rules.rs for why clusters/attached-unresolvable
# forms aren't recognised).
[[command]]
id = "git-commit-no-verify-short"
reason = "git commit -n/--no-verify skips pre-commit and commit-msg hooks"
command = "git"
required_tokens = ["commit"]
required_flags = ["n|--no-verify"]
value_flags = ["m", "message"]

# issue #146: `git-no-verify-any-subcommand` (a single required_flags-only
# rule spanning every git subcommand) used to live here. It's replaced by
# the explicit enumeration below because `-m`'s arity is subcommand-
# dependent (value-taking on commit/merge, boolean on rebase/am) — a single
# rule spanning all of git cannot safely declare `value_flags = ["m"]`
# without opening a hook-bypass hole on the subcommands where `-m` is
# boolean (confirmed: `git am -m "$(echo --no-verify)"` would wrongly Allow
# under a shared rule; `git rebase -m "$(echo --no-verify)"` would lose its
# own floor too, though the blanket `git-rebase` Block below still catches
# it regardless). Enumeration verified against `git 2.55.0`'s Main Porcelain
# commands (`man git-<subcommand>`, one at a time) for every subcommand
# that honors `--no-verify` at all:
#   commit, merge, pull, push, rebase, am
# `rebase` needs no rule of its own: `git-rebase` below already blocks
# every invocation unconditionally, regardless of flags. Every other Main
# Porcelain subcommand (fetch, clone, tag, branch, …) rejects `--no-verify`
# as an unknown option in this git version, so an unresolvable word in one
# of them no longer floors to Ask — re-audit this enumeration on git
# upgrades (a future subcommand could gain `--no-verify` support). One
# non-Porcelain exception is already covered explicitly below: `git p4
# submit --no-verify` (a Foreign Interfaces command, checked separately)
# also bypasses hooks.
[[command]]
id = "git-merge-no-verify"
reason = "git merge --no-verify bypasses pre-merge-commit and commit-msg hooks"
command = "git"
required_tokens = ["merge"]

[[command]]
id = "git-checkout-dashdash"
reason = "git checkout -- <path> discards uncommitted working-tree changes"
command = "git"
required_tokens = ["checkout"]
required_flags = ["--"]

# issue #452: `-f`/`--force` discards local modifications the same way the
# `--` spelling above does, but less unambiguously (a real `git checkout -f
# <branch>` genuinely does discard every local modification when
# switching, yet `-f` alone doesn't name a specific path the way `-- .`
# does) — Ask rather than Block. A flagless `git checkout .`/`git checkout
# <path>` is positionally indistinguishable from `git checkout <branch>`
# in rule data at all; `src/gate.rs`'s `git_checkout_or_restore_dot` covers
# the one case that's unambiguous regardless of position: an operand that
# lexically normalizes to `.` can never be a branch/commit-ish name.
[[command]]
id = "git-checkout-force-ask"
decision = "ask"
reason = "git checkout -f/--force discards local modifications when switching branches"
command = "git"
required_tokens = ["checkout"]
required_flags = ["f|--force"]

# issue #452: `git restore <path>` (no `--staged`) discards working-tree
# changes the same way `git checkout -- <path>` does; `git restore
# --staged <path>` alone only unstages (non-destructive). `required_flags`
# can express "the flag IS present", never "some flag OTHER than --staged
# is present" or "not only --staged" — so this asks on every `git restore`
# invocation, `--staged`-only calls included, rather than silently missing
# the destructive ones.
[[command]]
id = "git-restore-ask"
decision = "ask"
reason = "git restore <path> discards uncommitted working-tree changes (git restore --staged <path> alone is safe, but no rule shape here can require \"anything other than only --staged\")"
command = "git"
required_tokens = ["restore"]

# No required_flags: every invocation blocks unconditionally, which is also
# why the git-*-no-verify enumeration above has no git-rebase-no-verify —
# `--no-verify` on rebase (rebase's `-m` is boolean `--merge`, so it can't
# safely declare value_flags) is already covered by this blanket Block.
[[command]]
id = "git-rebase"
reason = "git rebase rewrites commit history"
command = "git"
required_tokens = ["rebase"]

# value_flags (issue #146, same reasoning as git-commit-no-verify-short
# above): without it, `git commit -m "$(...)"` would still Ask via THIS

[[command]]
id = "git-commit-amend"
reason = "git commit --amend rewrites the previous commit"
command = "git"
required_tokens = ["commit"]
required_flags = ["--amend"]
value_flags = ["m", "message"]
